query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high‐entropy alloys exposed above 900 °C, the ability to form and maintain a stable, coherent protective oxide layer is primarily governed by the nature of the added X element. When X = Al or Si, these elements promote the formation of slow‐growing, thermodynamically stable oxides (Al2O3 or SiO2) that form a continuous, adherent scale with lower cation diffusivity and reduced internal stress. In contrast, when X = Mn, its fast outward diffusion leads to the formation of volatile or porous manganese oxides that tend to crack or spall under thermal stress. In multiphase alloys, the distribution of secondary phases and higher grain-boundary density further aids in rapid formation and stress accommodation of these protective oxides, whereas in a single-phase solid solution, a uniform chemistry is the key to suppressing non-uniform diffusion and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys processed either as a single-phase solid solution or as a multiphase alloy with controlled microstructural heterogeneity.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the X element (substitute Si, Mn, or Al) into the CrFeCoNiX system and, independently, tailor the microstructure (single- vs. multiphase) to control diffusion pathways.
generation.conditions: Exposure to oxidative or corrosive atmospheres at temperatures above 900 °C (e.g., 900–1100 °C) for extended durations (e.g., 24–100 h) under controlled oxygen partial pressures.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, coherent oxide layer whose adhesion and integrity are mediated by the thermodynamic stability of the oxide species (e.g., Al2O3 or SiO2 versus Mn-oxides) and by the grain-boundary density that controls diffusion and stress relief in multiphase microstructures.
generation.mechanism: Al or Si additions lower the cation mobility and favor the nucleation and slow growth of protective oxides that exert less internal stress and minimize pore formation, thereby resisting spallation. In contrast, Mn’s rapid diffusion leads to the formation of volatile, non-protective oxides that develop porosity and cracking. In multiphase microstructures, enhanced intergranular diffusion accelerates the formation of a uniform protective layer that resists further oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Al or Si will develop a thinner, more coherent and adherent oxide scale with lower levels of cracking/spallation compared to alloys with X = Mn. This protective behavior is expected to be more pronounced in multiphase microstructures due to additional diffusion barriers at phase interfaces.
generation.baseline: A CrFeCoNiMn alloy, which typically develops thick, porous, and unstable Mn-rich oxide scales that crack and spall during high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys with near-equiatomic compositions, for both single-phase and multiphase states, when exposed above 900 °C in oxygen-rich or corrosive atmospheres. Effects may be sensitive to small variations in grain size, phase distribution, and exact environmental conditions.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis combines observations from studies on oxidation mechanisms in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni systems (e.g., evidence of Mn-driven unstable oxide formation in PMC10384371 and PMC11169556) with results showing improved oxidation resistance from Al additions in HEA systems (e.g., PMC9692591). The extrapolation to include Si is reasonable by analogy with Al due to its similar oxide benefits, but the exact role of Si versus Al remains less well defined, and the influence of microstructural phase distribution on stress accommodation is an additional uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy samples where X is systematically varied among Si, Mn, and Al. Fabricate specimens in both single-phase and multiphase states using identical processing routes. Subject all samples to isothermal oxidation tests at temperatures above 900 °C (e.g., 950–1050 °C) in a controlled oxygen-rich or corrosive atmosphere for extended durations (e.g., 24 to 100 h). Use in situ and ex situ techniques such as high-temperature XRD, SEM (with cross-sectional analysis), and thermogravimetric analysis to monitor oxide layer thickness, composition, coherence, and spallation events over time.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology (via SEM and TEM)
Phase composition of the oxide scale (via XRD and XANES)
Spallation events and adhesion quality (via microscopy and mass gain/loss measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with X = Al or Si do not exhibit a significantly thinner, more coherent, and less spall-prone oxide scale relative to the Mn-containing baseline under identical test conditions, or if the microstructural state (single-phase vs multiphase) does not alter the oxidation behavior as predicted, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

The initialisation and evolution of different oxide phases that were found with XRD scans agree well with these elements’ diffusion sequence order. Mn, Cr, and Fe preferentially diffused outward and became oxidized on the surface of specimens with time and temperature. The oxidation behaviour of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA provides valuable insights into its suitability for high-temperature applications. This oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi HEA plays a critical role in determining its mechanical, thermal, and corrosion resistance properties in elevated temperature environments. The observed non-protective oxide formation, particularly the depletion of Mn in the bulk alloy, can have significant implications for this particular alloy’s mechanical properties. Mn is known to contribute to solid solution strengthening and can enhance the mechanical strength and ductility of alloys. Therefore, the formation of non-protective oxides and the depletion of Mn may negatively affect the mechanical performance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA at high temperatures.

At temperatures exceeding 500 °C, the oxidation behavior of traditional and complex alloys (e.g., Ni-Cr, Ni-based superalloys, Fe-Cr, CoCrFeNiMn ‘Cantor’ alloy) has been extensively studied in oxygen-rich environments and over extended periods (from days to hundreds of days,). Key contributors to the process include species transport to the oxide/metal junction within the base alloy, movement across the oxide/metal interface, and passage through the oxide layer. For instance, atmospheric oxidation of CoCrFeNiMn-containing alloys results in a layered oxide film, with Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides attributed to outward cation diffusion. In a study by Kim et al., the high-temperature oxidation of FeCrMnNiCo (900–1100 °C in 20% O2/80% N2 for 24 h) showed the formation of layered Cr2O3 and Mn2O3 oxides at 900 °C. This process led to Ni, Fe, and Co enrichment in the base alloy. At 1000–1100 °C, the outer Mn2O3 layer changed to Mn3O4, forming a (Mn, Cr)3O4 ternary oxide with Ni, Fe, and Co in a solid solution. cited_evidence.text: In the case of the Mn15Al5 alloy, the outer part of the oxide layer was mainly composed of Mn, suggesting the presence of MnxOy oxides followed by a thin layer of Cr-based oxides found at the metal/oxide interface. Moreover, a significant level of porosity was found within its closest proximity of it. The overall thickness of the whole layer after 100 h annealing reached approximately 25 µm. More importantly, the Mn15Al5 alloy was the only one showing strong sub-surface oxidation and developed internal porosity due to the diffusion of Mn toward the oxide layer. It was found that the sub-surface porosity reached up to ≈100 µm into the alloy core and likely may further progress with the increasing time of annealing. The present oxides within the metal were mainly composed of Mn and Al. Increasing the content of Al above 5 at.% resulted in a completely different behavior, forming a well-protective oxide layer containing foremostly Al, suggesting the formation of AlxOy without any traces of chipping or formation of sub-surface oxides.
